paragraphs.text: These are fragments of [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) cakes pressed in Yunnan in the 1980s, broken from whole cakes and sold as loose pieces. That puts them in the style’s first two decades: the [wet-pile method](shou:wet-piling) only reached production in 1973.
At forty-one years, the pieces sit well within what the trade counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). Here storage shapes the tea as much as the years do.

brewing.text: The tea comes already broken, so there is no cake to work apart with a pick. Use boiling water, about 7 grams to 100 ml, one quick rinse, then short steeps that lengthen as the pieces open. Ripe tea forgives a heavy hand and gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.

unsupported.why: Plain arithmetic from 1973 (production start) to the 1980s gives roughly a decade or less to 15 years. 'First two decades' is a stretch, though 1980s is within 20 years of 1973 (1973 to 1989 is under two decades), so this is supported. However, 'pressed in Yunnan' is supported by origin. This flag is weak: the main concern is only whether 'the style's' is claimed beyond the wet-piling claim, which it is not.
